comment.value:
The paper introduces BEDLAM2.0, a large-scale synthetic dataset extending the original BEDLAM with significantly more realistic video data, diverse human subjects, and especially varied camera parameters (both intrinsics and motion trajectories). It includes detailed shoes, hairstyles, clothing, diverse body shapes (including high-BMI), and complex lighting conditions. Importantly, it integrates naturalistic camera shake, focal length variation, and motion capture types to better mimic videos “in the wild.”
Experiments show that training with BEDLAM2.0 (alone or combined with BEDLAM) improves human mesh recovery performance, both in camera and world coordinates, across several state-of-the-art models.

BEDLAM2.0 extends the original BEDLAM in several important aspects. It introduces varied focal lengths and realistic camera trajectories, including natural shake effects. The dataset covers a broader range of human body types, clothing, hairstyles, and shoes, enhancing robustness to shape and appearance variations. Motion sequences include more complex and rare cases. Rendering quality is also improved through varied lighting, HDRI environments, reflections, and detailed clothing features such as wrinkles. Together, these enhancements lead to consistent performance gains on both camera-space and world-space benchmarks when BEDLAM2.0 is used in training.

The main concerns raised in the initial reviews were mesh-penetrating motions, missing foot–ground contact, the absence of pathological or elderly motions, the lack of facial expressions and multi-person interactions, and the question that the paper overclaims improvements over SOTA methods without sufficient supporting data.

In the author–reviewer discussion phase, the authors adequately addressed the reviewers’ concerns by providing detailed explanations and additional experimental results. Based on this feedback, all reviewers recommended acceptance, and the AC also recommends acceptance.

Thanks for the comments. We will update the text to follow your suggestions.

----------

> The dataset lacks common occlusion phenomena frequently observed in real-world scenarios. In all instances, body parts remain fully visible without being occluded by objects, other people, or self-occlusion, which does not align with real-world data distributions.

The dataset actually includes a significant amount of occlusion, including frame occlusion, scene occlusion, self occlusion, and person-person occlusion, not to mention occlusion caused by clothing. Some examples can be found in the SupMat video: person-person occlusion (0:04+) and scene occlusion (0:10+ top/right, 0:16+). We will make sure to select more examples for the paper and video that illustrate this. 

We performed a quantitative analysis on a randomly selected set of 41.5k images (covering 58.6k rendered bodies) to examine occlusion due to frame, scene and person-person. Our results show that 12.7% of images exhibit more than 20% occlusion, and the top 10% most occluded bodies experience an average of 61.1% occlusion.

----------

> It also lacks representations of human-object interactions. Even in actions such as handstands, the contact between the hands and the ground is not realistically modelled.

This is true and we mention this in line 330. Addressing this is very challenging. We will make this limitation more clear.

Thank you for recognizing the value of B2 for training and for the detailed questions about this. We will address all your suggestions in the revised manuscript as summarized below.

----------

> 1.1 The distribution of focal lengths used for rendering is said to be “inspired by the statistics of focal lengths collected from Flickr,” but the process for determining the final distribution is not described.

We will add a plot comparing our field-of-view histogram with those used in the CameraHMR paper.

> 1.2. The relationship between synthetic camera motions and captured real camera motions remains unclear. Specifically, it is not stated how frequently each is used.

This is stated in the supplementary webpage of statistics but we will mention this in the text as well. The answer is 86.4% synthetic, 13.6% motion capture.

----------

> The authors claim that “training on B2 (or B1 + B2), with no real data, achieves world-space accuracy exceeding the recent SOTA.” Premature conclusion? Include the performance of GVHMR and PHMR when trained on mixed datasets as a fair comparison.

Thanks for pointing this out. B1+B2 alone gives better accuracy than reported in the original GVHMR and PHMR papers. Here are the numbers for comparison

| Models                          | WA-MPJPE | W-MPJPE | RTE  | Jitter | Foot-Sliding |
|-------------------------------|----------|---------|------|--------|---------------|
| GVHMR (original paper)        | 111.0    | 276.5   | 2.0  | 16.7   | 3.5           |
| GVHMR w. B1+B2                | 109.7    | 273.1   | 1.7  | 15.0   | 3.4           |
| PHMR (original paper)         | 71.0     | 216.5   | **1.3**  | 16.3   | 3.5           |
| PHMR w. B1 + B2               | **70.5** | **193.7** | 1.4 | **11.3** | **3.2**     |

Note that the original GVHMR and PHMR versions both use B1 as well as some real data. Both are improved by the addition of B2 and we suspect real data will result in further improvement.

We will add these numbers to Table 2 and expand the discussion.

----------

> In scenes with multiple people, their motions appear to lack temporal or semantic coherence. 

We mention this in line 331 but will make this clearer. 

----------

> How can people visualize the ground-truth labels/annotations? Can the BEDLAM visualization tools be reused here?

The scripts provided in the original BEDLAM repo are compatible with BEDLAM2. We will release additional visualization tools for BEDLAM2.

----------

> I encourage the authors to consider releasing the motion retargeting code.

Thanks for the suggestion. We are happy to release the retargeting code.

----------

> Will the assets, such as clothes, hair,, and shoes, and the rendering pipeline, be made open-source or available upon request? 

The short answer is “yes” and we will make this clearer. The clothes, hair, and shoes will be released on our download server. We will also make the body textures with the bald scalps available. The only assets that we are not able to distribute are the 3D environments and we provide a “shopping” list so people can get these themselves (see SupMat Table 3). Code for evaluation, training and rendering will be released on GitHub, similar to our previous work BEDLAM.

We thank the reviewer for the positive comments and attention to detail. We will address all your suggestions in the revised manuscript. 

----------

> In samples featuring barefoot individuals (e.g., seq191 of 20240614_5_200_citysamplenight_tracking), proper foot-ground contact is sometimes missing, causing the character to appear as if floating.  

Indeed, in this scene, the ground is not flat but tilted. We chose to have the bodies a bit above ground in these cases so that they do not penetrate the ground during motion. We will create a document with known issues so that users can exclude sequences that do not fit their needs.

----------

> Although the proposed hairstyles add diversity and enhance the realism of the videos, it is unclear how this contributes to 3D human pose and shape estimation.

The reviewer may well be correct but we expect people to use this dataset for a variety of tasks such as training or evaluating avatar creation from images or video. For tasks like this, hair will be valuable.

----------

> Despite the diversity of human motions, the dataset includes only healthy individuals and does not capture pathological movements, such as stooped posture in elderly people using canes or walkers.

In the limitation section, we will point out that the body shapes and motions do not cover the full range of the population.

----------

> Human motions in BEDLAM2.0 are independent and lack coordinated multi-person interactions, such as dancing, which are covered in [1] along with camera movement.

The motions of each person are sampled individually. Because we sample motions from AMASS, we do not have multi-person sequences with contact. We will state this as a limitation and point to WHAC as a source for such motions.

Thanks for recognizing the value of the dataset to the community. We are happy to adopt your suggestions as explained below.

----------

> There's a lack of facial animations. For example, upper body or full body talking footage like TED talks, or face-to-face conversations.

True. We will add this to the limitations section.

----------

> I wonder if self-hosting is a good idea. The limitation of single-threaded downloading of BEDLAM was already painful. Now there's 26TB data. Wouldn't it take forever to download?

- We agree that it should be a simple process for the end-user to get access to the provided data and also in a reasonable timeframe. To address this, we provide download scripts to let people only download subparts of the dataset. Out of the 26TB data, 15TB is for depth data that many people don’t need. If video compression is not an issue, then one can just download the MP4/H.264 videos (160GB) instead of the PNG images.
- We provide a dedicated email address bedlam@tue.mpg.de where we actively monitor user feedback. Our inhouse IT service is continually improving the data access quality and has now set up a new data download server for BEDLAM2. 
- We will improve the download situation by exploring additional hosting options if our current uplink speed becomes a bottleneck.

----------

> Will the checkpoints of the methods (PromptHMR) trained on B2 be released?

Yes.

----------

> How many 4090 GPU hours are consumed for generating the dataset?

- Thanks for this question. We will add this information to the paper. 
- Rendering: Based on collected render statistics for the dataset, it took less than 467h (383h PNG, 84h depth) to render all the provided training set image data.
  - We initially rendered on an RTX 3090 GPU (60% of generated PNG images) and later switched to an RTX 4090 GPU (40% of generated PNG images), so GPU hours for the RTX4090-only GPU render setup will be lower.
  - The observed GPU utilization varied from 30% to 100%, with HDRI renders (highly GPU-bound) with complex hair grooms having the highest GPU utilization.
- The clothing simulations were performed using CLO fashion design software on machines equipped with Intel Xeon CPUs operating at frequencies between 2.0 and 2.5 GHz. Each simulation utilized 12 CPU cores, as using a higher number of cores was found to degrade performance. Under this configuration, simulations—ranging from 120 to 480 frames in length—required an average of 0.8 hours to complete. A total of 10,592 simulations were generated for the training and test datasets, resulting in approximately 8,579 CPU hours on 12-core, 2.0–2.5 GHz processors.
- We will include these details in the SupMat.

----------

> It would be ideal if for every video the corresponding T-pose/A-pose/DA-pose was recorded in meshes. Might be useful for avatar generation tasks.

For BEDLAM, we distributed every body in clothing in A-pose. We will add that to BEDLAM2 as well. Thanks for the suggestion. Every combination of a body shape and outfit can be generated. The hair is a problem though since it is a strand-based groom and not a simple mesh so we would do this without hair.

----------

> Also, it might be useful to record rendered normal and position maps, for downstream tasks like normal estimation, dense pose, single image to 3d human, etc,.

Adding world-space or camera-space normal images would greatly increase the dataset size. We will provide this functionality as part of the render pipeline so people can generate these themselves if they want them.

summary.value: The paper introduces BEDLAM2.0, a large synthetic video dataset designed to include realistic camera movements and a wide range of human motions in different environments and lighting conditions. Unlike earlier synthetic datasets, BEDLAM2.0 adds realism with features like natural hairstyles, varied clothing, and a variety of shoes that maintain proper contact with the ground. Experiments on SOTA models show that using BEDLAM2.0 in the training data can enhance the methods in both camera coordinates, due to increased diversity and realism, and world coordinates, due to varied camera motions and motion capture types.

strengths_contributions.value:
- The first large-scale dataset with varied focal lengths and camera motions, while still being realistic.

- By adding diversity in human subjects, such as high-BMI body types and more 3D clothing outfits, the dataset is well-suited for improving model robustness to variations in body shape and clothing.

- The dataset features diverse camera motions and motion capture types in varied locations and includes shake effects to mimic how videos are captured in the wild.

- It covers complex and rare motions (e.g., sequence 15 in 20250219_3-4_250_middleeast_vcam_approach), diverse lighting conditions (e.g., seq0 vs. seq9 in 20250110_1_250_chemicalplant_vcam), HDRI environments, and realistic visual cues (such as reflections of people in seq14 of 20240709_5_250_archmodelsvol8_zoom, or dress wrinkles responding to movement in seq11 of 20250212_1_250_yakohama_upperbody).

- In addition to proposing a large-scale synthetic dataset with camera motions, BEDLAM2.0 also emphasizes physical plausibility by removing actions that require interaction with objects (e.g., sitting or stair climbing) from the pool of human motions, and by including shoes with proper foot-ground contact.

- Evaluations in both camera space and world space show a clear improvement in human mesh recovery when BEDLAM2.0 is used in training data.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- Samples (rarely) show artifacts (e.g., a hand going inside the shirt in sequence 8 of 20241107_1_250_archmodelsvol8_tracking, or hair penetrating a hoodie from the outside in sequence 18 of 20240708_1_250_ai0901_static_portrait). - In samples featuring barefoot individuals (e.g., seq191 of 20240614_5_200_citysamplenight_tracking), proper foot-ground contact is sometimes missing, causing the character to appear as if floating.

- Although the proposed hairstyles add diversity and enhance the realism of the videos, it is unclear how this contributes to 3D human pose and shape estimation.

- Despite the diversity of human motions, the dataset includes only healthy individuals and does not capture pathological movements, such as stooped posture in elderly people using canes or walkers 

- Human motions in BEDLAM2.0 are independent and lack coordinated multi-person interactions, such as dancing, which are covered in [1] along with camera movement.


[1] Yin et al. "WHAC: World-grounded humans and cameras" ECCV 2024.

summary.value:
The authors propose BEDLAM2.0 as a new training dataset for the Human Pose Estimation problem.

Compared to existing datasets, its primary novelty lies in the variation of camera parameters, including both intrinsic properties and camera motion.

Compared to BEDLAM (B1), BEDLAM2.0 (B2) is enhanced with more diverse body shape, motions, clothing, hair, and 3D environments and added with shoes.

The experiments (test on real-world dataset) provide evidences of:

1.	Training on B2 (or B1 + B2) is significantly better than training on B1.

2.	New methods (GVHMR and PHMR) trained on B1 + B2 are better than previous method trained on mixed datasets.

strengths_contributions.value:
[Contributions] 

Mainly, compared to the existing dataset, the main difference is the variation of the camera parameters (both intrinsic and motion). Additionally, the method for capturing real camera motions is both practical and potentially useful for future datasets."
In addition, B2 is extended from B1 by expanding the scale and diversity of the data in terms of body shapes, motions, footwear, clothing, hairstyles, and 3D environments. Although the paper does not provide ablation studies to isolate the impact of each individual factor, several of these enhancements are intuitively beneficial. For instance:

1.	Various body shapes may reduce the network’s tendency to estimate average body shape.

2.	Shoe modeling can provide more reasonable human-ground interactions.

3.	Variability hairstyles adds to the realism of the dataset. 

[Effectiveness] 

The experiment shows the enhancement of training on B2 (or B1+B2) against training on B1 alone.

[Organization] 

The paper is well written and clearly structured. The Figures clearly illustrate the distribution of camera FoVs and camera motions.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
[1. Clarity of Some Details] Several implementation details are insufficiently explained. 

1.1. The distribution of focal lengths used for rendering is said to be “inspired by the statistics of focal lengths collected from Flickr,” but the process for determining the final distribution is not described.

1.2. The relationship between synthetic camera motions and captured real camera motions remains unclear. Specifically, it is not stated how frequently each is used.

[2. Potentially Overstatement？]

The authors claim (lines 327–328) that “training on B2 (or B1 + B2), with no real data, achieves world-space accuracy exceeding the recent SOTA.”

However, this conclusion appears premature, as the comparisons are made between GVHMR / PHMR trained on B2 and recent SOTA methods (e.g., DPVO+HMR2.0, GLAMR, TRANCE, SLAHMR, WHAM) trained on mixed datasets. Since GVHMR and PHMR themselves are recent methods not introduced in this paper, it is unclear whether the performance gain is due to the new dataset or the strength of the methods themselves.

The authors should clarify why they do not include the performance of GVHMR and PHMR when trained on mixed datasets as a fair comparison.

[Minor, Limited Realism in Multi-Human Motion Scenes]

In scenes where multiple people are placed together, their motions appear to lack temporal or semantic coherence. The combined actions do not exhibit any shared intent or interaction, which reduces the realism and plausibility of such scenes.

[Minor, Data Usability for Reviewers]

It is not clear how reviewers can visualize the provided ground-truth labels. While the authors state that the camera and motion data formats are “similar to” those used in BEDLAM (CVPR 2023), they do not clarify whether the same visualization tools can be reused, or whether any tools or scripts are provided to assist in this process.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

ethical_comments.value:
There are no or only very minor ethics concerns because:

The human body models are parametric and non-identifiable.

Although real-world camera motions were captured using handheld devices, no visual data or private environments were recorded—only device motion data was used.

dataset_code_comments.value:
The dataset appears to be complete and consistent with what is described in the main paper. The authors have provided the data in a standard and usable format, and it is readily downloadable. I was able to inspect a sample sequence without difficulty, and the data structure seems well-organized.

However, I could not find a tool for rendering or projecting annotations, which would have been helpful for verifying their correctness in a short time.

additional_feedback.value:
I encourage the authors to consider releasing the motion retargeting component as part of the public toolkit. This would enable researchers to transfer motions among SMPL/SMPL-X model sequences more easily and could help increase adoption and citations of the dataset.

Additionally, I would like to ask, will the assets used in this work—such as clothes, hairs, and shoes, and the rendering pipeline—also be made open-source or available upon request? I understand some of them are commercially purchased, but I still encourage the authors to release assets and tools as possible, which would further benefit the community and also increase the impact of this work.

final_justification.value:
Thanks the authors for their detailed response. I appreciate that my main concern has been directly addressed: the comparison showing that GVHMR/PHMR trained on B1+B2 outperforms the same methods trained on B1+real data.

﻿ I'm also glad to hear that the authors plan to release the motion retargeting tools and the human assets, which will increase the practical value and impact of the dataset. Other implementation details I had questions about have also been clearly clarified in the response.

﻿ Overall, I find the paper solid and valuable. It provides clear empirical evidence: simply using this new dataset can lead to measurable improvements in human pose estimation, regardless of the specific method.

﻿ After careful consideration, I have decided to keep my original score (5). My reasons are as follows:

- My original score has already assumed that the authors would address my major concerns.
- The dataset does not quite represent a transformative shift.

summary.value: BEDLAM2.0 is an extended version of the BEDLAM dataset, featuring a wider range of camera motions and enhanced realism in aspects such as hairstyles, clothing styles, and especially the inclusion of detailed shoes. Compared to BEDLAM, it offers higher fidelity and precision. However, the dataset lacks representations of human-object interactions. For instance, during actions like handstands, the contact between hands and the ground lacks realism. Additionally, common real-world phenomena such as occlusions are underrepresented, making some scenarios less consistent with real-life situations.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. BEDLAM2.0 is a large-scale synthetic humans dataset that offers a wider range of camera motions and includes more diverse viewpoints. It also features a greater variety of hairstyles, clothing styles, and more detailed hand representations.
2. It addresses the lack of focus on shoes in the original BEDLAM dataset by introducing multiple types of shoes in BEDLAM2.0, making it more realistic.
3. Compared to BEDLAM, BEDLAM2.0 demonstrates improved performance in predicting human poses in real-world scenarios.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The dataset lacks common occlusion phenomena frequently observed in real-world scenarios. In all instances, body parts remain fully visible without being occluded by objects, other people, or self-occlusion, which does not align with real-world data distributions.
2. It also lacks representations of human-object interactions. Even in actions such as handstands, the contact between the hands and the ground is not realistically modelled.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

final_justification.value: Your rebuttal has addressed some of my concerns; however, the lack of human-object interactions still remains. Therefore, I will maintain my score of 5.

summary.value:
This is paper presents BEDLAM2.0, the massive improvement over the popular BEDLAM dataset.

Various limitations in BEDLAM are addressed by the newly proposed BEDLAM2.0 dataset.

The impact of this dataset to the community is for sure.

strengths_contributions.value:
The ill-estimation of camera parameters has proven to be one of the major sources of error. BEDLAM2.0 covers a wide range of focal length variations, as well as camera trajectories.

Hair and shoes, which are missing in BEDLAM, are well addressed in 2.0.

More clothes assets.

More diverse body shapes.

Generation is improved from images to videos.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
There's a lack of facial animations. For example, upper body or full body talking footage like TED talks, or face-to-face conversations.

I wonder if self-hosting is a good idea. The limitation of single-threaded downloading of BEDLAM was already painful. Now there're 26TB data. Wouldn't it take forever to download?

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: Dataset is available on the website.

additional_feedback.value:
Will the checkpoints of the methods (PromptHMR) trained on B2 be released?

title.value: BEDLAM2.0: Synthetic humans and cameras in motion

TLDR.value: BEDLAM2.0 is a significant expansion of the popular BEDLAM dataset that increases pose and body shape variation, adds shoes, and, most importantly, introduces a wide range of realistic cameras and camera motions.

abstract.value: Inferring 3D human motion from video remains a challenging problem with many applications. While traditional methods estimate the human in image coordinates, many applications require human motion to be estimated in world coordinates. This is particularly challenging when there is both human and camera motion. Progress on this topic has been limited by the lack of rich video data with ground truth human and camera movement. We address this with BEDLAM2.0, a new dataset that goes beyond the popular BEDLAM dataset in important ways. In addition to introducing more diverse and realistic cameras and camera motions, BEDLAM2.0 increases diversity and realism of body shape, motions, clothing, hair, and 3D environments. Additionally, it adds shoes, which were missing in BEDLAM. BEDLAM has become a key resource for training 3D human pose and motion regressors today and we show that BEDLAM2.0 is significantly better, particularly for training methods that estimate humans in world coordinates. We compare state-of-the art methods trained on BEDLAM and BEDLAM2.0, and find that BEDLAM2.0 significantly improves accuracy over BEDLAM.  For research purposes, we provide the rendered videos, ground truth body parameters, and camera motions. We also provide the 3D assets to which we have rights and links to those from third parties.
